Abstract
Late-interaction models like ColBERT offer a competitive perfor-
mance across various retrieval tasks, but require storing a dense
embedding for each document token, leading to a substantial in-
dex storage overhead. Past works address this by attempting to
prune low-importance token embeddings based on statistical and
empirical measures, but they often either lack formal grounding
or are ineffective. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a
framework grounded in hyperspace geometry and cast token prun-
ing as a Voronoi cell estimation problem in the embedding space.
By interpreting each token’s influence as a measure of its Voronoi
region, our approach enables principled pruning that retains re-
trieval quality while reducing index size. Through our experiments,
we demonstrate that this approach serves not only as a competi-
tive pruning strategy but also as a valuable tool for improving and
interpreting token-level behavior within dense retrieval systems.

1 Introduction
Late-interaction retrieval models such as ColBERT [ 16,24] and
COIL [ 10] have emerged as a powerful paradigm for neural in-
formation retrieval. By representing documents and queries as
sets of token-level embeddings and computing relevance via fine-
grained token interactions, these models capture lexical and seman-
tic matches that are often missed by single-vector encoders such as
DPR [ 15]. This expressivity enables strong retrieval effectiveness
while maintaining competitive latency [23].
However, this performance comes at a substantial cost. A late-
interaction model stores an embedding for every document token,
resulting in indexes that are orders of magnitude larger than those
of sparse or single-vector dense retrievers. At realistic corpus scales,this storage overhead becomes a fundamental bottleneck, limiting
deployability and increasing both memory and compute costs.
To reduce the index size, several works propose index compres-
sion techniques. For instance, ColBERTv2 [ 24] leverages a linear
projection to reduce the vector representation to a smaller dimen-
sion. Meanwhile, it also leverages the residual quantization to fur-
ther reduce the storage required for each document token vector.
However, not all token embeddings contribute equally to re-
trieval. Many tokens are weakly informative, only relevant for
vanishingly small sets of queries or encode redundant informa-
tion [ 11], suggesting that pruning uninformative tokens can reduce
storage while minimally impacting retrieval performance. Concep-
tually, this is analogous to how removing the token “The” from the
sentence “The capital of France is Paris” would have virtually no
impact on the information conveyed.
Existing approaches attempt to prune tokens by typically relying
on heuristics or learned signals, often with insufficient principled
backing.Learning-free methodsoften exploit linguistic or statistical
signals, such as stopword lists, IDF scores, or token positions within
a document [ 1,20]. For instance, early tokens or content words
with high IDF values are retained, while low-IDF tokens such as
“the” or “and” are discarded. These methods are simple and model-
agnostic, making them easy to deploy across different retrieval
architectures. However, they ignore the interaction between tokens
and queries in the embedding space. A token that is statistically
“unimportant” may still be critical for distinguishing relevant from
non-relevant documents for certain queries. In contrast,learning-
based approachespropose neural modules based on proxy signals
to inform pruning decisions. For instance, AligneR [ 22] proposed
to employ entropy-regularized optimization (relaxed top- 𝑘opti-
mization), and ColBERTer [ 13] reduces the number of vectors by
combining sub-word vectors into unique whole-word representa-
tions and learns to discard them through a trainable gate vector.
However, they provide limited theoretical backing, and very little
work has focused on formalizing the pruning objective itself.
To our knowledge, Zong and Piwowarski [27] are the first to
propose a formally defined lossless token pruning objective, aimed
at removing only those tokens that do not affect retrieval scores.
Although conceptually elegant, their experimental results demon-
strate that achieving truly lossless pruning is extremely challengingarXiv:2603.09933v1  [cs.IR]  10 Mar 2026

Kankanampati et al.
in practice. Their experiments further show that applying this loss-
less objective in a lossy setting where a fixed subset of tokens must
be retained can lead to substantial degradation in retrieval perfor-
mance, particularly at very high pruning ratios. Additionally, their
formulation requires document vectors to be of non-unit norms,
further limiting its applicability.
We address the aforementioned limitations by introducing a
principled and practical framework that formalizes the pruning
objective in terms of expected retrieval error using hyperspace ge-
ometry. In this framework, we demonstrate that the importance of
a token embedding can be accurately characterized by its Voronoi
region [ 2] in the embedding space, which represents the set of
query tokens for which that token is most important. Building
on this characterization, we derive a pruning algorithm that effi-
ciently identifies tokens that can be pruned from a document while
minimally impacting retrieval performance, by directly optimizing
the pruning objective that other approaches attempt to indirectly
approximate, resulting in pruning that minimizes retrieval degra-
dation, even under aggressive pruning where as many as 90% of
the tokens in a document are removed.
Beyond these improvements, our approach offers a new analyt-
ical perspective on token-level relevance, shedding light on the
geometry of embedding spaces and their role in retrieval.
Our main contributions are as follows:
(1)We reframe the ColBERT token pruning as a Voronoi cell
estimation problem, and demonstrate that the pruning ob-
jective and strategy proposed are highly effective and versa-
tile. More precisely, compared to approximated LP-pruning
from [ 27], our proposed approach is about 120 times faster
while being more principled.
(2)We evaluate our pruning algorithm using varying pruning
ratios, regularization strengths, and domains, demonstrat-
ing versatility, effectiveness, and strong generalization.
(3)We highlight the broader utility of the formalism by using
it to analyze empirical approaches such as first- 𝑘token
pruning and demonstrating the linear relationship between
mean error (MER) and retrieval impact (nDCG@10), which
can be used to guide pruning decisions.
Collectively, our contributions establish a principled theoretical
framework for token pruning while demonstrating its practical
effectiveness in late-interaction retrieval.
Given the widespread adoption of ColBERT as a standard late-
interaction architecture, we conduct all experiments within this
framework to provide a controlled and comparable evaluation of
pruning behavior. While our empirical results are instantiated in
this setting, the proposed formulation depends only on the max-sim
aggregation mechanism and the geometry of the embedding space,
and therefore extends naturally to other late-interaction models.
The code for the pruning algorithm and associated experiments
is publicly available on GitHub1.

Late-interaction Retrieval.Late interaction models represent doc-
uments and queries as sets of token-level embeddings and comput-
ing relevance via fine-grained token interactions. With transformer-
based architectures, late-interaction models rely on simple interac-
tion mechanism and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Models
like ColBERT [ 16,24] or its variants [ 10,18,19] compute query-
document relevance by computing the highest inner product of the
representation for each query token with that of a document token
representation. Although such models allow to build an index for
first-stage retrieval, they still require huge index sizes compared to
single vector models. To alleviate such problems, index compression
and index pruning methods have been proposed.
Index Compression.A first approach to reduce the index size,
which is orthogonal to our work, focuses on compressing embed-
dings rather than pruning them. Models such as ColBERT and
ColBERTer [ 14] reduce the dimensionality of token embeddings
directly using linear projection layers. ColBERTv2 [ 24], CRISP [ 26]
and [ 6] cluster token representations to either fully replace to-
ken embeddings or significantly reduce their size. MUVERA [ 4]
similarly compresses token representations into fixed-dimensional
encodings that approximate multi-vector similarity. On a related
note, XTR [ 5] and PLAID [ 23] also optimize retrieval latency by fil-
tering token clusters using query-cluster dot products, using similar
geometric constraints as clustering approaches.
Although index compression reduces vector size, it retains redun-
dant vectors. Index Pruning can remove these redundant, low-utility
vectors, cutting storage and compute costs.
Index Pruning.Past pruning approaches can broadly be classi-
fied as learning-free or learned methods. Learning-free methods
apply heuristic criteria such as removing stopwords [ 1], low-IDF
tokens [ 1,20], retaining first- 𝑘tokens, or attention-based prox-
ies [17,20]. These approaches do not require additional training,
enabling straightforward, model-agnostic pruning. Learn-based
methods, on the other hand, employ auxiliary modules to iden-
tify low-utility tokens. ConstBERT [ 21] uses a fully connected
layer to prune a document into a fixed set of embeddings, while
LeapMV [ 12] applies a fully connected layer with a Gumbel-softmax
gate to produce discrete token-level pruning decisions. AligneR [ 22]
further frames multi-vector retrieval as a sparse alignment problem,
jointly learning token salience and pairwise document–query inter-
actions. More closely related to our work, [ 27] prunes tokens that
do not affect the similarity score, framing their identification as a
linear programming (LP) problem. However, the paper falls short
as a destructive dimensionality reduction is necessary to achieve
good pruning ratio, and LP is computationally demanding, making
the method inapplicable for large document collections. We show
that our proposition yields a much better effectiveness-efficiency
trade-off than the above mentioned works.

4.2 Voronoi Pruning Algorithm

now outline Voronoi Pruning, the algorithmic procedure that takes
advantage of this measure to produce optimally pruned token sub-

(1) Monte Carlo Estimation of Expected Error;
(2) Iterative token removal with error updates;
(3) Global application across documents;
(4) Search strategies to improve beyond greedy selection.

Iterative Pruning.Pruning is inherently structural, and removing
a token reshapes the surrounding Voronoi cells, altering the contri-
bution of neighboring tokens. A one-shot strategy that evaluates
token errors only once may, therefore, yield suboptimal subsets. To
address this, we adopt aniterative pruning scheme. At each iteration,
the token with the smallest current pruning error is removed and
the error estimates of all remaining tokens are recomputed under
the updated Voronoi diagram. This adaptive update ensures that
subsequent decisions reflect the evolving structure of the represen-
tation space and leads to higher-quality pruned sets. The need and
effect of this strategy are illustrated in Figure 2, where iterative
pruning (Figure 2c) preserves a lower mean error in the maximum
dot-product values compared to non-iterative pruning.
The iterative nature of our algorithm is practically manageable
for two reasons. Firstly, when a document token is pruned, only
the queries previously assigned to its Voronoi cell need to be reas-
signed; the membership of other query vectors remains unchanged.
Secondly, most computations involved rely on dot-product opera-
tions, which are highly optimized on modern GPUs. Consequently,
although iterative updates introduce considerable computational
overhead, an efficient implementation allows the approach to scale
easily to large datasets with minimal difficulty.
Global Pruning.Because our pruning error is consistently de-
fined across all documents, we extend the procedure to operate at
thecollection level. Instead of pruning independently within each
document, tokens are ranked globally by their error contributions,
and the lowest-impact token is removed at each step until a tar-
get budget (e.g., a fixed number or fraction of tokens) is reached.
This allows for more efficient identification and pruning of low-
importance tokens at thecollection level.

computationally intractable combinatorial problem. Although our

5.2 Datasets
The in-domain accuracy of our Voronoi Pruning (VP) approach
is evaluated using the MS MARCO v1 passage retrieval task [ 3].
The tasks consists of 8.8M passages paired with real user queries
and relevance annotations, and serves as our primary benchmark
for evaluating pruning effectiveness. For in-domain evaluation, we
report the MRR@10 scores on the MS MARCO dev set consisting

Kankanampati et al.
of 6,980 queries. Additionally, we also evaluate our approach on the
2019 (43 assessed topics) and 2020 (54 assessed topics) iterations of
the TREC Deep Learning track [ 7,8], which also utilize the 8.8M
passage corpora from MS MARCO. To assess robustness under
domain shift, following common practice, we additionally evaluate
in a zero-shot setting on the same subset of the BEIR benchmark [ 25]
as earlier works. We report the MRR@10 for the MS MARCO dev
set, and nDCG@10 for TREC-DL and BEIR.
5.3 Baselines
We compare our methodology against a diverse set of baselines that
span both traditional information retrieval approaches and recent
state-of-the-art developments. Specifically, we include:
Retrieval Baselines.- We compare our approach against three
widely used, unpruned retrieval baselines. BM25 is a classical lexical
matching baseline and remains a widely adopted reference in IR
research due to its simplicity and strong empirical performance.
SPLADEv2 [ 9] is a state-of-the-art learned sparse retriever that is
also used as a first-stage retriever in our re-ranking experiments.
We also include the performance metrics of ColBERTv2 [ 24] be-
fore our pruning algorithm and fine-tuning routine are applied,
in both its end-to-end configuration and re-ranking setup. In the
end-to-end setting (ColBERTv2-e2e), we use the original configu-
ration of ColBERTv2, building an index and retrieving the docu-
ments in a single stage using PLAID [ 23]. In the re-ranking setup
(ColBERTv2-rerank), we re-rank the top 1000 documents retrieved
by SPLADEv2 using ColBERTv2. This enables a direct comparison
with late-interaction retrieval performance and quantifies the ex-
tent to which effectiveness is preserved under various scoring and
pruning strategies.
Static Pruning Strategies.- We compare against four heuristic-
based methods for token pruning: stopword removal, low-IDF prun-
ing, positional pruning, and attention score-based pruning.
Learned Pruning Strategies.- We further compare against
learned pruning approaches, which dynamically identify and reduce
low-importance tokens through additional modules that typically
require fine-tuning. Approaches such as AligneR [ 22] attempt to
predict pruning decisions on a token-level to decide which tokens
to retain, whereas ConstBERT [ 21] aims to represent document
tokens using a fixed number of embeddings. ColBERTer [ 13] is
another such learned pruning approach that proposes to reduce the
size of token embeddings while retaining the original size of [CLS]
token embeddings, resulting in an overall reduction of the index
size. We also compare against the dominance-based pruning and
regularization framework introduced by [ 27], which formulates
pruning as the elimination of token embeddings that are redun-
dant under vector dominance constraints. In particular, we report
comparisons against two of the strongest pruning strategies in-
troduced in that work, namely Norm Pruning (NP), which prune
the document token which has a norm smaller than a threshold
𝜃=0.5, and LP-Pruning (LPP), which prune the document token
that diagnostically has a low contribution to the query-document
token interaction, with a threshold𝜃=0.7.The selected baselines are highly diverse, motivated by differ-
ent paradigms (including linguistic, mathematical, and neural ap-
proaches) and differ widely in computational costs, fine-tuning
requirements, and overall versatility. By evaluating our proposed
approach against this set of baselines, we present a comprehensive
understanding of its strengths and limitations.
6 Results and Analysis
6.1 Main Results
6.1.1 In-domain retrieval.Table 1 reports MRR@10 on the MS
MARCO dev set under varying pruning strategies. Among all learning-
free methods, Voronoi Pruning achieves the highest effectiveness
while maintaining comparable pruning ratios, preserving 98.0% of
the unpruned ColBERTv2 end-to-end performance at a 50% token
budget and convincingly outperforming heuristic baselines such as
IDF-based, positional and attention-score pruning.
Voronoi Pruning approaches the performance of other learned
pruning methods, such as AligneR, at moderate pruning ratios, de-
spite operating entirely post hoc without additional fine-tuning or
architectural modifications. When applied to a ColBERTv2 check-
point fine-tuned with the doc-sim and L1 regularizers, Voronoi
Pruning also competes with the strongest learned pruning strate-
gies, including Norm-Pruning and LP-Pruning, matching their ef-
fectiveness. However, unlike Norm-Pruning and LP-Pruning, our
method can also be applied directly to embeddings with unit norm,
increasing its applicability across different pre-trained models.
Moreover, we note that Voronoi Pruning achieves this competi-
tive performance while being substantially faster than LP-Pruning.
Using 10,000 sample points, it processes 10,000 documents in 12.0
seconds, compared to 1,474.3 seconds for LP-Pruning - a 120×
speedup. This combination of strong effectiveness, broad applicabil-
ity, and exceptional efficiency underscores the practical advantages
of Voronoi Pruning for both moderate and aggressive token pruning
scenarios.

modest even at aggressive pruning levels, indicating robustness
under domain shift.
In several datasets (e.g., FiQA, NFCorpus, and TREC-COVID),
Voronoi pruning closely matches or exceeds the performance of
more expensive learned pruning approaches. These results suggest
that a geometry-aware pruning objective generalizes better across
domains than heuristic or token-position-based strategies, which
are often sensitive to dataset-specific token distributions.

Effect of Beam Size.In principle, beam search could help bridge
the gap between our greedy pruning strategy and the global opti-

Global vs Local pruning.Pruning can be done on either a document-
level or the corpus-level. When pruning at the corpus-level, we
compare pruning error scores across documents, and prune those
with the smallest scores before updating the scores to reflect the
new pruned space. It must be noted that in both settings, the scores
are still calculated at the document-level, and pruning a token vec-

very little difference between the execution times for global and
local pruning.

namic pruning can be theoretically useful, it is a relatively compute-
heavy process. As such, we investigated the performance gained by
dynamically updating the scores after pruning each vector, against
a pruning setup where only the initial pruning error scores were
used for deciding pruning candidates, hereby referred to as the

than pruning a single token per iteration and recomputing errors
each time, we prune multiple tokens at each step, thereby reduc-

step size of 3, this strategy results in an almost threefold speedup,

6.3 A Mean Error Perspective on First- 𝑘Pruning
The first-𝑘pruning strategy [ 20] is motivated by the observation
that tokens appearing earlier in a sequence often contribute most to
ColBERT scores for a fixed set of queries. While this method works
reasonably well in practice, its underlying assumptions and limita-
tions can be better understood through our Mean Error framework:
Mean Error vs. Score Contributions.First- 𝑘pruning estimates
token importance based on maximum dot-product contributions
and observes that earlier tokens tend to be more influential. How-
ever, when we measure token importance using a sample of MS
MARCO’s train set as described in [ 20], the mean error calculated
across sampled query vectors, a more relevant metric for analyzing
pruning, we find that the distribution is much less skewed. While
early tokens can have higher individual contributions, the mean
error reveals a relatively more balanced view of which tokens can
be safely pruned, as illustrated by Figure 4.
Identifying the lack of iterative pruning.First- 𝑘pruning applies
a static selection of tokens without updating for how the contribu-
tions of remaining tokens change as others are removed. Following
our discussion in 4, it is readily apparent that First- 𝑘pruning per-
forms a single-step, non-iterative pruning. And by calculating mean
errors after pruning every token, we can easily see why this non-
iterative nature of First-k pruning is suboptimal.

view of token importance by computing a pruning rank for each
token within its document, normalizing ranks by document length,
and grouping tokens by their relative position percentile. Aggregat-

charts highlights the variability in token importance with respect to

6.4 Guiding Pruning Decisions with Mean Error
We study the relationship between theMean Error(ME) induced in
document representations and retrieval effectiveness under varying
pruning ratios. Using Voronoi Pruning, we observe a strongly linear
relationship between ME and nDCG@10, with an 𝑅2value of0.99
across TREC-DL19 and TREC-DL20, and0 .91on the TREC-COVID
dataset (Figure 6). This indicates that ME serves as a highly reliable
proxy for post-pruning retrieval performance.
This strong correlation enables a practical pruning strategy:
rather than tuning pruning ratios directly against retrieval met-
rics, one can select a target ME threshold to achieve a desired
efficiency–effectiveness trade-off. Importantly, this behavior aligns
with our geometric interpretation of ColBERT scoring—pruning
that induces low ME preserves high-volume Voronoi regions that
dominate similarity aggregation, resulting in minimal performance
loss. As a result, Mean Error provides a principled and computa-
tionally efficient criterion for guiding pruning decisions.
7 Conclusion
We introduced Voronoi Pruning, a principled framework for token
pruning in late-interaction retrieval models grounded in the geome-
try of embedding spaces. By casting pruning as the minimization of
expected retrieval error and interpreting token importance through
Voronoi regions, our approach directly optimizes the objective that
prior methods approximate indirectly.
Across in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations, Voronoi Prun-
ing consistently achieves strong effectiveness–efficiency trade-offs,
matching or outperforming learned pruning methods while remain-
ing entirely post hoc and orders of magnitude faster than prior
optimization-based approaches. Crucially, our method remains ro-
bust under aggressive pruning for in-domain tasks, where heuristic
and dominance-based strategies degrade sharply.
Beyond its empirical performance, Voronoi Pruning provides a
powerful framework for understanding token-level relevance in
late-interaction models, enabling both principled pruning and new
analytical insights into existing heuristics.
That said, our framework also has important limitations. Since
our pruning criterion relies on mean error, which captures the

Addressing these limitations opens several promising directions
for future work. In particular, our geometric formulation could be
extended to incorporate distribution-aware or worst-case error ob-
jectives, tighter alignment with task-level retrieval losses, or learn-

their prunability. This could potentially aid in developing prunable
models for out-of-domain data retrieval, where robustness under
domain shifts remains a challenge. We leave these directions to
future work and hope that the framework introduced here enables
more principled analysis, probing, and optimization of embedding
spaces in neural retrieval systems.

structure.title: Problem Formulation
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel approach called "Voronoi Cell Formulation for Principled Token Pruning" for late-interaction retrieval models, specifically addressing the challenge of efficiently pruning document tokens without significantly impacting retrieval relevance scores.

The core problem is to identify and remove document tokens that contribute minimally to the relevance score, which is calculated using a ColBERT-like formulation: $ColBERT(Q,D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q \cdot d$.

The document builds upon prior work that defines pruning as removing tokens that never achieve the maximum inner product for any query. However, it acknowledges the practical difficulty of achieving perfectly "lossless" pruning, as most tokens contribute to the maximum score for at least some queries.

To overcome this, the paper proposes a relaxed pruning objective: finding a subset of document tokens of a predetermined size $k$ that minimizes the error introduced by pruning. This error is defined as the expected difference in the maximum similarity score between the original document and the pruned subset, averaged over all possible queries.

The methodology then introduces the concept of a "Voronoi cell" for each document vector, defined as the set of query vectors for which that document vector is the top-scoring match. The error introduced by pruning a single vector is then related to the queries within its Voronoi cell.

The paper outlines a "Voronoi Pruning Algorithm" with four main components:
1.  **Monte Carlo Estimation of Expected Error:** Since direct computation of the expected error is intractable, it is approximated using Monte Carlo sampling of query vectors.
2.  **Iterative token removal with error updates:** The algorithm iteratively removes tokens based on their estimated error.
3.  **Global application across documents:** The pruning is applied to documents in a broader context.
4.  **Search strategies to improve beyond greedy selection:** The paper aims to go beyond simple greedy approaches to find better pruned subsets.

The document also provides empirical evidence supporting the assumption of a uniform distribution of query embeddings, which is crucial for the Monte Carlo estimation of expected error.

nodes.title: Voronoi Pruning Algorithm
nodes.summary:
The document introduces a novel method called "Voronoi Cell Formulation for Principled Token Pruning" for late-interaction retrieval models, specifically building upon the ColBERT architecture. The core problem addressed is how to efficiently prune document tokens without significantly impacting retrieval accuracy.

The main points covered are:

*   **ColBERT Retrieval Score:** The document starts by defining the ColBERT retrieval score as a sum of maximum inner products between query tokens and document tokens.
*   **Previous Pruning Approaches:** It discusses prior work on token pruning, particularly "Lossless Pruning" [27], which aims to remove tokens that never contribute to the maximum inner product for any query. However, it highlights the practical difficulty of achieving perfect lossless pruning.
*   **Proposed Relaxed Pruning Objective:** To overcome the limitations of exact lossless pruning, the authors propose a relaxed objective: finding a subset of tokens of a predetermined size `k` that minimizes the error introduced by pruning. This error is defined as the expected difference in retrieval scores between the original and pruned sets of document tokens.
*   **Voronoi Cells:** The methodology introduces the concept of Voronoi cells for document token vectors. A Voronoi cell `Vi` for a document vector `di` is defined as the set of query vectors for which `di` is the top-scoring match. This partitions the query space based on which document token is the best match.
*   **Error Measurement:** The error introduced by pruning a single token `di` is defined as the expected decrease in the maximum similarity over all queries, specifically focusing on the queries within `di`'s Voronoi cell.
*   **Voronoi Pruning Algorithm:** The proposed algorithm, "Voronoi Pruning," consists of four key components:
    1.  **Monte Carlo Estimation of Expected Error:** Due to the intractability of direct computation, the expected error is approximated using Monte Carlo sampling of query vectors, assuming a uniform distribution.
    2.  **Iterative Token Removal:** Tokens are iteratively removed, starting with the one that has the smallest estimated pruning error. After each removal, the error estimates of the remaining tokens are recomputed to account for the changing Voronoi diagram.
    3.  **Global Application:** The pruning process is applied globally across all documents in a collection, rather than independently within each document, to identify and prune low-impact tokens more effectively.
    4.  **Search Strategies:** To improve beyond a simple greedy selection, the paper explores beam search as a strategy to explore multiple candidate pruned subsets and potentially find better solutions.
*   **Justification for Uniform Sampling:** The document provides empirical evidence (Figure 1) showing that query embeddings, even from real-world datasets like MS MARCO, exhibit distributions that justify the assumption of uniform sampling for Monte Carlo estimation.
*   **Confidence Intervals:** The paper discusses the challenges and feasibility of estimating confidence intervals for the pruning error, highlighting that the cell membership probability is well-behaved.
*   **Experimental Setup:** Details on implementation, including the use of pre-trained ColBERTv2 checkpoints, comparison with existing regularization methods (L1 norm, Doc-sim), and the number of sample points used for error estimation.
*   **Ablation Study on Beam Search:** The paper notes that beam search, while explored, was found to be impractical due to memory overhead and computational slowdowns, with no significant improvement in performance. Therefore, most experiments omit beam search.
*   **Datasets:** The MS MARCO v1 passage retrieval task is used as the primary benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed Voronoi Pruning approach.
*   **Illustrative Example:** Figure 2 visually demonstrates the benefit of iterative pruning over non-iterative pruning using a 2D example.

*   **Analysis of First-k Pruning:** The document critiques the "first-k pruning" strategy, highlighting its limitations by analyzing token importance through a "Mean Error" framework. It argues that first-k pruning's static, non-iterative approach is suboptimal compared to more dynamic methods.
*   **Mean Error as a Pruning Metric:** The core of the proposed approach, Voronoi Pruning, is introduced. It leverages "Mean Error" (ME) as a proxy for retrieval effectiveness. The document demonstrates a strong linear relationship between ME and retrieval performance (nDCG@10), suggesting ME can guide pruning decisions for efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs.
*   **Voronoi Pruning Framework:** The framework is described as principled, grounded in the geometry of embedding spaces, and aims to minimize expected retrieval error. It is presented as an improvement over prior methods that indirectly approximate this objective.
*   **Empirical Evaluation and Performance:** Voronoi Pruning is shown to achieve strong effectiveness-efficiency trade-offs, outperforming other pruning methods on various benchmarks (e.g., BEIR). It is noted for its speed and robustness, especially under aggressive pruning.
*   **Limitations and Future Work:** The document acknowledges limitations of the current Mean Error criterion, such as not accounting for heterogeneous error distributions and being purely selection-based. Future directions include developing distribution-aware or worst-case error objectives and learning procedures that shape embedding spaces for better prunability.
*   **Figures and Tables:** The text references figures illustrating token contribution to scores and mean errors (Figure 4), pruning timing relative to token position (Figure 5), and the relationship between Mean Error and retrieval performance (Figure 6). Table 3 provides comparative nDCG@10 scores for different pruning strategies on BEIR benchmarks.
